questions.question: Which of the following statements best explains the concept of equivalence partitioning as described in the provided material?

options.A: It divides all possible test inputs into groups where each group is expected to produce identical results, so testing one member of a group is sufficient.
options.B: It requires testing every possible input value individually to guarantee complete coverage.
options.C: It focuses only on invalid inputs and ignores valid input ranges.
options.D: It is used solely for performance testing, not functional testing.

questions.explanation:
Equivalence partitioning groups inputs that are expected to behave the same way, allowing a single test case per group; this is stated on [Page 44] where input partitions are defined and processed identically.

---

questions.question: According to the context, why might a tester create a separate input equivalence partition that only shares the characteristic of producing outputs in the same output partition?

options.A: To reduce the number of test cases by merging valid and invalid inputs.
options.B: Because some inputs, although different, lead to the same type of output and can be tested together.
options.C: To ensure that every possible output is tested with every possible input.
options.D: To comply with validation testing guidelines that require unique inputs for each output.

questions.explanation:
The text notes that a separate input partition may be defined when the only common characteristic is that they generate outputs within the same output partition [Page 44].

---

questions.question: In validation testing, test cases are selected to reflect the system’s expected use. How does equivalence partitioning support this type of testing?

options.A: By deliberately selecting obscure inputs that are unlikely to be used in practice.
options.B: By dividing the expected input domain into representative groups and choosing typical values from each.
options.C: By focusing exclusively on boundary values without considering middle values.

questions.explanation:
Validation testing uses realistic inputs; equivalence partitioning helps by identifying input partitions that reflect normal usage and selecting representative cases from each [Page 36] and [Page 44].

---

questions.question: A function under test accepts a numeric code that can be 0, 1, or any integer greater than 1. Which set of equivalence partitions correctly captures the valid and invalid input domains?
questions.explanation:
The context describes partitioning inputs into valid groups (e.g., specific values and a range) and a separate invalid group (e.g., non‑numeric). This matches the example of distinct valid partitions plus an invalid partition [Page 44].

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship that can exist between input and output equivalence partitions?

options.A: Each input partition must map to multiple unrelated output partitions.
options.B: There is always a one‑to‑one mapping between every input and output partition.
options.C: Sometimes a single input partition corresponds to a single output partition, but not always.
options.D: Input partitions and output partitions are unrelated concepts.

questions.explanation:
The material notes that sometimes there is a 1:1 mapping between input and output partitions, but this is not guaranteed [Page 44].

questions.question: When performing defect testing, how might a tester use equivalence partitioning differently from validation testing?

options.A: By selecting only the most common inputs from each valid partition.
options.B: By creating partitions that include obscure or unlikely inputs to expose hidden defects.
options.C: By avoiding any invalid input partitions.
options.D: By testing every single value in each partition.

questions.explanation:
Defect testing aims to expose defects and may use obscure inputs; equivalence partitioning can still be applied by defining partitions that contain such atypical values [Page 36].

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an invalid input equivalence partition as described in the context?

options.B: All strings that are longer than 255 characters.
options.C: All negative numbers when only non‑negative numbers are allowed.
options.D: All dates in the future for a system that only processes past dates.

questions.explanation:
The text mentions that the shaded area representing invalid inputs forms an equivalence partition; negative numbers in a non‑negative domain are a typical invalid partition [Page 44].

questions.question: How does equivalence partitioning help reduce the number of test cases needed for a component?

options.A: By requiring that every possible input be tested at least once.
options.B: By allowing the tester to select one representative value from each partition, assuming all members behave the same.
options.C: By focusing only on boundary values and ignoring interior values.
options.D: By eliminating the need for any test cases that target invalid inputs.

questions.explanation:
The core idea is that members of a partition are expected to be processed identically, so one test per partition suffices [Page 44].

questions.question: A software component processes a string input that must be exactly 5 characters long, consisting only of uppercase letters. Which equivalence partitions should a tester define?

options.A: Valid: {5‑character uppercase strings}; Invalid: {all other strings}.
options.C: Valid: {uppercase strings of any length}; Invalid: {non‑uppercase strings}.
options.D: Valid: {5‑character strings}; Invalid: {strings of other lengths}.

questions.explanation:
The description fits an input partition where the valid class is the exact requirement, and everything else forms a single invalid partition, matching the notion of partitions in the text [Page 44].

questions.question: In the context of equivalence partitioning, what is meant by the statement “a program being tested should process all of the members of an input equivalence partition in the same way”?

options.A: The program must produce identical output values for every member of the partition.
options.B: The program must execute the same code path for every member of the partition, leading to equivalent behavior.
options.C: The program must reject all members of the partition as invalid.
options.D: The program must treat the partition as a single input value.

questions.explanation: The text explains that members of a partition are expected to be handled similarly, implying the same processing logic or code path [Page 44].
